entries.title: Justice Department issues subpoenas to California election workers
entries.summary: Grand jury subpoenas sent to election workers in Los Angeles come amid escalating tensions between the Trump administration and California election officials over the state's voter rolls.
entries.content:
Justice Department issues subpoenas to California election workers

The Department of Justice issued subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles in an escalation of tensions with California election officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.

The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office confirmed to NPR on Thursday that it received grand jury subpoenas directed at employees last week.

The confirmation follows reporting that first appeared in the The New York Times that at least two employees at the registrar's office were served grand jury subpoenas with instructions to appear in court on Nov. 4.

In recent weeks, the DOJ sent letters to local election officials in California warning them they could "risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure" if they refuse to cooperate with DOJ demands to set aside ballots pertaining to people that federal officials have flagged as "likely" noncitizens.

"If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime," the letters warned.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment about the subpoenas.

It is unclear whether the staff who received the subpoenas are the targets of a criminal investigation at this point.

The news of last week's subpoenas comes a day after a federal judge in California rejected a request by the Justice Department to require California election officials to set aside and stop processing the ballots of thousands of California voters who appear on a list of 20,000 names federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter found there was no legal basis for the DOJ's demand and the court was not convinced its list was reliable. The judge also raised concerns the effort would disenfranchise eligible voters and create election chaos.

The DOJ is appealing his ruling to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

At a hearing in Carter's courtroom on Tuesday, the judge warned Justice Department officials, "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately."

Carter repeated that message in the order he issued Wednesday evening, writing: "The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop."

Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan expressed gratitude for Carter's comments in a statement Thursday.

"Judge Carter's admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated," Logan said. "At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law."

He added: "We will take whatever steps necessary to ensure the safety of our employees and to remain focused on serving the voters of Los Angeles County so they can exercise their voting franchise."

entries.title: Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate
entries.summary: New reporting alleging Democratic efforts to prop up a spoiler candidate has roiled Alaska's all-important U.S. Senate race.
entries.content:
Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate

Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.

That story detailed efforts by Democratic campaign operatives to recruit what Republicans have long alleged is a spoiler candidate whose presence on the ballot could confuse voters and siphon support from the GOP incumbent. The two candidates share the name Dan Sullivan.

NPR hasn't independently confirmed the Times' reporting, but it's roiled the Senate race just days before Election Day. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is hoping to flip the seat for her party.

The Times' story is based on interviews and communications among Peltola's attorneys and advisers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Democrats have long denied involvement in the non-incumbent Sullivan's candidacy, and both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC reiterated those denials after the Times story published.

While campaigning Wednesday, Peltola called the story a distraction, according to Alaska Public Media, and the non-incumbent Sullivan did not respond to Alaska Public Media's requests for comment. He has previously said it was his decision to run for Senate.

Republicans have pounced on the news.

"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan, said in a statement. President Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election loss, called the Alaska findings "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level," in an online post.

Trump's Justice Department had already sought to intervene in the Senate race, asking a court last week to delay certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a small margin. The legal effort cited potential voter confusion stemming from the second Sullivan on the ballot.

Election law experts had broadly derided the DOJ's case as weak, in part because the Constitution grants states control over elections.

The Sullivan candidacies had already been probed by state officials, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the non-incumbent Sullivan could appear on the general election ballot.

Justice Department officials said Thursday the Times' story expands its options for investigating the Senate race, and it filed an amended complaint citing the new reporting.

And in the wake of the Times story, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said Wednesday night that he is directing the state's Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

It's unclear what laws could have been violated.

Trickery has been fairly common in politics, and it can be difficult to write laws that prevent shenanigans, according to Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who's co-authored a book on dirty tricks in campaigns.

"There's just a lot of tricks," Kamarck told NPR. "There's old ones. There's new ones. In this day and age, the internet makes it really easy to get the word out, both on a trick or, frankly, on a correction to a trick. But it's pretty standard fare for campaigns."

At times major-party advisers will seek to boost third-party candidates, in an effort to undercut the other major-party's candidate. Some voters who spoke with Alaska Public Media compared the new reporting about the Sullivan case to Republican groups' spending in support of a Democrat who's a federal prisoner in New York but who's on Alaska's U.S. House ballot.

The second, non-incumbent Sullivan advanced to the general election after Alaska's nonpartisan primary that sends the top four vote-getters to the fall ballot.

Alaska Public Media found mixed reactions to the Times' reporting, with some residents frustrated that it's drawing attention from other issues, and others expressing skepticism that voters would be confused. The ballot notes which Sullivan is the Republican incumbent.

Some experts have pointed out that all the news about the second Sullivan's candidacy could reduce any voter confusion. And because the state has a ranked-choice voting system for the general election, if voters are confused, they could rank both Sullivans and not rank Peltola.

Whether voters want to keep the state's unique election system is also on the general election ballot.

NPR's Hansi Lo Wang and Ryan Lucas contributed reporting.

entries.title: Patrick Stewart, a perceptive patriarch in 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men,' dies at 86
entries.summary: Stewart was raised by an abusive father but became best known for playing kind, paternal leaders who united families of misfits.
entries.content:
Patrick Stewart, a perceptive patriarch in 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men,' dies at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart's most famous characters tackled concepts such as honor, morality and courage. He played Professor X in the X-Men franchise and Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the starship USS Enterprise, on the show Star Trek: The Next Generation and its later spinoff, Picard.

Stewart died Wednesday at 86. A post on his Facebook and Instagram pages said he died at home in Los Angeles after a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."

Although he was beloved for playing compassionate father figures who united families of misfits, Stewart's own upbringing in Yorkshire, England, was harsh. He remembered his father as alcoholic and abusive. He found solace in school and, eventually, in Shakespeare. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and debuted on Broadway in 1970 in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

"To stand in the middle of an empty stage in an empty theater and feel that I was at home was everything," he told NPR in 2023. "But it took a while for me to get there."

Stewart played alongside some of the best Shakespeareans of his time, including Judi Dench and Ian McKellen. He was lecturing on Shakespeare at UCLA when his name came up for the lead in a new series of Star Trek.

"Don't do this, Patrick," he remembered McKellen advising him. "You're a very good stage actor. That's where you ought to be. Don't do it."

But Stewart's agent had reassured him that the show was unlikely to make it past the first season. As the actor recalled to NPR, he was encouraged to take what he believed to be a quick and easy job. "'Do six months' work. Make some money for the first time in your life and get well known. Get a suntan, and go home.' And I thought, 'Yeah, that doesn't sound too bad. I could live with that.'"

But Star Trek: The Next Generation was a tremendous hit. It aired for seven seasons, from 1987 to 1994. Stewart was embraced by fans, who adored the character's penchant for Earl Grey tea and cool-headed leadership, with such signature phrases as "Engage!" and "Make it so!"

But success on the starship Enterprise came at a cost. Throughout his career, Stewart portrayed only a handful of Shakespeare's leading men. He put some of that character energy into an award-winning, one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, in which Stewart played more than 40 roles.

By the beginning of the 21st century, Stewart had reestablished himself on stage while also lending his voice to numerous big-budget animated films. He went on to dominate another blockbuster franchise, the X-Men, beginning in 2000. He'll appear for the last time in his role as Professor Charles Xavier in the upcoming movie Avengers: Doomsday.

As for his signature role, Stewart thought he was done playing Picard. But a team of producers — including writer Michael Chabon — had different ideas. They pitched him a new show, Star Trek: Picard, that began streaming on the CBS service now called Paramount+ in 2020.

"I would've been happy just shaking Patrick Stewart's hand and telling him how much I loved him on Star Trek," Chabon told NPR. "But to be able to actually write words that he will speak and act is — it's incredible."

In the show, Picard is struggling with the psychological damage that led to leaving Starfleet. The performance is vintage Stewart. His character is keen-eyed, haunted, weary, yet joyful. While this Picard was trapped in the past, Patrick Stewart spent his career charting the future.

Correction Oct. 29, 2026

This story has been updated to remove a photo of Patrick Stewart in character as Jean-Luc Picard that had been reversed by the agency that provided it.

entries.title: Some rural Republicans in California say redistricting has left them without a voice
entries.summary: California's far northeastern corner used to be a reliably red congressional district. But Proposition 50 carved it up, meaning many voters there may soon have a Democrat representing them in D.C.
entries.content:
Some rural Republicans in California say redistricting has left them without a voice

California's far northeastern corner used to be a reliably red congressional district. But Proposition 50 carved it up, meaning many voters there may soon have a Democrat representing them in D.C.

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

In the far northeastern corner of California...

(SOUNDBITE OF COW MOOING)

CHANG: ...Where about four dozen cows are gathered around me, staring at me dead in the eye.

(Laughter) I feel like I'm teaching a class of cow students or something.

We're in Modoc county, where the cows vastly outnumber the humans. I mean, there are only two people per square mile around here.

NED COE: Come boss. Come boss.

CHANG: That's Ned Coe. He's been ranching up here for decades. He still uses the same cattle call that his dad used to use back in the day. What are you actually saying? Come, comma, boys?

N COE: Come boss.

CHANG: Oh, boss.

N COE: Bossy. Bossy.

CHANG: Oh, right.

N COE: Come boss.

CHANG: Come boss.

We're in Modoc County because Californians voted overwhelmingly for Prop 50 to redistrict the state and gain five more Democratic seats. And so, after 13 years of being represented by a Republican farmer, Ned and his wife, Valerie, are probably going to be calling a Democrat from the San Francisco Bay Area their new congressman, Jared Huffman.

VALERIE COE: When a politician, his base of voters live in the city and they don't identify with our way of life, they don't understand our way of life, he is going to make decisions that benefit them, and no consideration will be given to us because it can't be. He needs their votes.

CHANG: And voters in Marin County, where Huffman is based, make up 30% of the vote in this district, whereas Modoc County makes up just 1%.

V COE: And they know that we're a very small minority up here, and we're largely Republican. So pragmatically speaking, he's not going to spend time on the issues that are devastating our local economies, our small...

CHANG: Issues, Valerie says, like all the laws protecting gray wolves, which keep attacking the cattle and other livestock up here.

V COE: A wolf is not in the least bit afraid of a human being. The only thing that protects us is a firearm, and you're not allowed to use a firearm against them.

CHANG: Do you think that the legal protection that lawmakers give to gray wolves reflects a bias against your way of life?

V COE: Absolutely. This is our business. This is our way of life, and we're not allowed to protect ourselves. I mean, to know that your horse is out in the backyard being eaten by a wolf and you can't even run that pack of wolves off, and you have other horses out there.

CHANG: It seems unfair to you.

V COE: It's cruel. We care very deeply about these animals. We pride ourselves on being good stewards of the land and being good stewards of our animals.

CHANG: And that love of animals is evident right back at the Coes' ranch house, where Valerie's paintings of horses and farm life decorate the walls.

V COE: Would you like any sugar or...

CHANG: Oh, no, thank you.

This cattle country went solidly for President Trump in the last three presidential elections. And even though Ned and Valerie Coe are Republicans themselves, they don't like their party's role in the redistricting fight.

V COE: What was done in Texas was wrong. Two wrongs do not make a right. It was done, and the advantage went to the Republicans. It's still not right. And in California's case, the advantage goes to the Democrats. Again, it's still not right.

CHANG: And Ned says this redistricting battle has only made his job as a county supervisor here harder. He now thinks the only way he can deliver for his community is to bypass his own congressional representative.

N COE: My approach has been to work with congressional members, whether they're from other parts of California or other states, that will help carry issues forward.

CHANG: You feel that you should go work with representatives of other districts in order to make sure that your interests are taken into account?

N COE: Yes.

CHANG: Yes. To people like the Coes, this new congressional map does count their votes - yeah - but only enough to ensure that they are politically discounted. To guarantee that this new district goes blue, a vast swath of it stretches along the entire Oregon border. Then a skinny tendril shoots down the California coast to land at the San Francisco Bay. It would take you something like 12 hours of nonstop driving to travel all that. And we do feel a bit of that trek as we make our way three hours west of the Coes' ranch, deep into timber country to meet Tristan Allen, who's a logger.

TRISTAN ALLEN: This is the Christmas tree heaven right here.

CHANG: Is that a noble fir?

ALLEN: We call him Shasta fir, but that's a noble fir.

CHANG: Because...

ALLEN: You paid top dollar for that Christmas tree.

CHANG: I did (laughter). That's my...

ALLEN: My...

CHANG: ...Favorite kind of Christmas tree...

ALLEN: And my wife...

CHANG: ...Is the noble fir.

ALLEN: My wife calls them Charlie Brown trees. She hates them. And I...

CHANG: Allen's entire logging business relies on these giant machines which allow a single worker to pull down 2,000 trees every day.

Oh, my God these trees look like toothpicks...

ALLEN: Yeah, yeah.

CHANG: ...In the jaws of that machine.

ALLEN: Yeah, it's about 150 feet tall.

CHANG: Oh.

ALLEN: And then he grabs it, and he throws it down where he wants it.

CHANG: Boom. It smells like Christmas right now.

ALLEN: There you go.

CHANG: Allen's logging operation burns through roughly 4,000 gallons of diesel per day. And the war in Iran has pushed up diesel prices so much Allen is in the red this year. But he says he would never give up his way of life here in Siskiyou County. His family goes back five generations here, and even though he's always felt at home in Siskiyou, Allen says he's always felt forgotten by California.

ALLEN: I like to refer to Siskiyou County as Baja, Oregon. And as derogative (ph) as that may be, no one in Oregon wants us and no one in California cares about us. So we have to figure out how to be heard and make sure that they pay attention. We need to leverage our natural resources so that we can demonstrate to them that we are something...

CHANG: Relevant.

ALLEN: There you go. That's a great word. Relevant. They need us. But until I convince them that they need us, they don't want us.

CHANG: Do you identify as a Californian if..

ALLEN: Oh, yeah.

CHANG: OK.

ALLEN: A hundred percent. A hundred percent.

CHANG: OK.

ALLEN: Northern California. I just had a meeting in Canada two weeks ago, and they were saying Bay Area people are saying there from Northern California, and then I...

CHANG: That's what I say.

ALLEN: Yeah, you're from Northern California.

CHANG: Yeah.

ALLEN: Well, you're central California, sweetheart.

CHANG: (Laughter).

ALLEN: I'm from Northern California. I'm 22 miles away from Oregon (ph).

CHANG: This feeling that Allen has of being dismissed, of being almost invisible here in Northern California, Allen says that feeling has only gotten worse since the new district line shoved him, a Republican, in with those so-called central California Democrats in the San Francisco Bay Area. It's a feeling that we heard all over here, from the cattle pastures to the timberlands, as well as along the muddy banks of Bogus Creek, only about 7 miles from the Oregon border. That's where we met up with rancher Ryan Walker.

RYAN WALKER: If you're going to catch any fish, you'll often see him coming through. We call this...

CHANG: This little creek is a tributary of the mighty Klamath River. You can sometimes see salmon fighting their way up from the Pacific Ocean to spawn here.

WALKER: The female salmon will make a nice little nest, and the male salmon will fertilize the eggs, and then they'll both die.

CHANG: So they don't even, like, do anything together when that fertilization is happening. And then they die after the whole thing.

WALKER: Yeah, after the whole thing, and then...

CHANG: Man, it's miserable to be a salmon.

WALKER: Then you can walk up the - well, you know...

CHANG: Walker's family has been ranching up here for 50 years. First sheep, then cattle. He's a registered independent, and I asked him, how does he feel about the torturous shape of his new district?

WALKER: I mean, of all the redistricting wars that have gone on, you're standing in what is clearly the most ridiculous district to be drawn. You know, the person who lives in Cedarville and the person who lives in - on a houseboat in Sausalito are entirely different thought process. It's just flat out not good politics because how do we go to a town hall in Sausalito...

CHANG: (Laughter).

WALKER: ...Or how does Sausalito come to a town hall in Alturas and have any kind of meaningful discussion to hash out issues? We're not a real district. This district was drawn with the purpose of making my voice less powerful. That's what gerrymandering is.

CHANG: But all of this begs a question. When you live in a sparsely populated area, how strong of a political voice should you be entitled to in a representative democracy?

WALKER: So, yes, we live in California. It's got some big urban centers that are going to drive policies for the state. You've created this state that's larger than a country, that has so many diverse issues going on. And so it becomes very unfair. I don't know that I think my voice should be outsized because I'm rural and sparse, but at the same time, there does have to be a voice.

CHANG: Any advantages to this redistricting that you could see?

WALKER: So, yeah, what - as the saying goes, ill wind indeed that doesn't blow some good. And is there a silver lining? Yeah, I think there is. Now the wolf area is going to be split among four maybe light blue districts. You know, there's going to be more congresspeople with wolf issues in their district, so perhaps there'll be a greater desire to find a comprehensive solution. For our district, the one advantage is that the entire California portion of the Klamath River is now in the same district. And there is a traditional friction between coastal communities and upland tributary communities.

CHANG: I mean, what you're saying is the Klamath River is an example of how when you consolidate conflicting interests, sometimes that can actually force a compromise outcome.

WALKER: Sure. It - well, and it just brings a force to the table that wasn't there before.

CHANG: So who are you going to vote for in November for your congressperson?

WALKER: Well, I think, as we just said, the whole point of Prop 50 was make my vote not count. So what does it matter?

CHANG: (Laughter).

WALKER: I mean, realistically.

CHANG: Are you really not going to vote?

WALKER: Oh, I'll vote on things that matter. I mean...

CHANG: But not District 2 congressperson?

WALKER: Oh, I mean, it's such a foregone conclusion at this point. It's just - it's not even...

CHANG: In fact, Walker struggled even to recall the last name of the Republican candidate in the congressional race, who's trailing way behind the Democrat.

(SOUNDBITE OF BALMORHEA'S "BOWSPRIT")

CHANG: By the way, that Democrat, Jared Huffman, he gave us a call. He says he plans to, quote, "Work hard to show up and listen to people in Modoc and Siskiyou counties" and in the other places he hopes to represent. He's taking a 950-mile road trip up there this week.

(SOUNDBITE OF BALMORHEA'S "BOWSPRIT")

entries.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
entries.summary: The penguins that perished lived on the Danger Islands in Antarctica. The prime suspect was avian flu. Researchers were surprised by what they found.
entries.content:
What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery

Sailing toward the Danger Islands, Dr. Ralph Vanstreels had a good idea of what he might find: A lot of dead Adélie penguins.

It was March 2024 and a virus had been sweeping through the area, leaving deceased birds in its wake.

Vanstreels got the crime right but the culprit wrong. There were dead penguins but a virus was not to blame.

As his vessel pulled up to a landing ramp on one of the islands — located just off the Antarctic Peninsula — Vanstreels and his fellow researchers immediately noticed bumps in the snow.

"Was each bump a rock or was it a carcass? We had to do quite a bit of intensive searching [through the snow]," says Vanstreels, who is based in Argentina and is a wildlife veterinarian with the University of California, Davis.

The team ultimately found more than 537 penguin carcasses on just the ramp, which he estimates was about the size of an airport runway.

There were many more carcasses elsewhere on the Danger Islands, which are home to two mega colonies for penguins. The researchers estimate there were thousands of dead Adélie penguins and other species of birds. But they had to work quickly and couldn't do a complete count, Vanstreels says.

"You cannot stay there very long because you might be locked down with an iceberg blocking your way out," he says.

As the team has pieced together this tragic penguin mystery, Vanstreels says, the case holds broader lessons for tracking the spread of diseases globally.

The only continent to dodge the virus — until now

Now let's time jump to Australia a few months ago for another bird disease conundrum.

In June, H5N1 — high pathogenicity avian influenza also known as bird flu — arrived in mainland Australia. Up until that point, Australia had been the only continent to dodge the virus which has traversed the globe, leaving a trail of carcasses in its path.

Since late 2021, the virus has led to the death of nearly 300 million poultry birds. Either the virus killed them or they were culled as a preventive measure to stop the spread of the disease, according to the World Animal Health Information System. Further, bird flu is estimated to have killed millions of wild animals and marine mammals, although it's hard to get an exact figure.

Researchers were amazed that Australia could stay bird-flu-free for six years. And the virus didn't take the path that scientists expected.

"We have a lot of migration of birds between Australia and Southeast Asia, so for the first few years, we're like: That's where the virus is coming from," says Dr. Amandine Gamble, an assistant professor at Cornell University in the Department of Public and Ecosystem Health.

The way bird flu eventually got there was from the other direction. It came from Antarctica likely via migrating birds.

"This is a virus that's not assisted by airplanes," Michelle Wille, senior research fellow at the Center for Pathogen Genomics at the University of Melbourne, told NPR in 2025. "This is a virus that's traveling by mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality."

"The virus loads are low"

So when Vanstreels set sail to check on the penguins, he assumed bird flu would be the culprit.

Bird flu arrived in Antarctica in late 2023 and early 2024. Vanstreels and his colleagues rapidly arranged for a trip to try to figure out exactly what was happening.

"The expedition was initially fully set up to look for bird flu because that was the panic," he explains, adding that ongoing fear of a continuing global panzootic — or pandemic among animals — is justified.

In several layers of warm clothes covered by protective gear — double gloves, coveralls, glasses and masks — Vanstreels and the team started taking samples of the penguin corpses they found.

"We looked a little bit stiff when walking — like a penguin walking almost — because of all the gear," he says. "We had very strict biosafety standards."

They brought samples from the deceased penguins back to a mini-lab on their boat. By evening, they had early results. But not the results they expected.

"There is bird flu here, but the virus loads are low," he recalls. "That was a little bit puzzling."

The carcasses were not very old, so Vanstreels would have expected to find far more bird flu virus if that had killed the birds. Perhaps something else was the main driver? "We were unsure what was happening," he recalls.

What the microscope revealed

So what killed the 500-plus penguins on the landing ramp and the many others on the island?

Back on land several months after the voyage, in the Netherlands, Vanstreels' colleagues did more investigation. "Under the microscope, you can see that there's bacteria in the tissues," he says — not virus.

They discovered a different disease, a bacterial disease that causes avian cholera (which is distinct from human cholera).

Vanstreels and his team's findings were published in October in the journal the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

So how worried are they about avian cholera?

The disease is not considered a major threat to humans since the strain that is specialized to birds is distinct from the strain specialized to mammals. "The risk for human infection is not really that high when you see an outbreak on birds," Vanstreels says. But, it does kill birds worldwide — especially in cold environments where the bacteria thrives.

While there's not enough research to know exactly how common avian cholera is, the disease has been on the radar of scientists for decades. However, it's not exactly top of mind. The last time researchers looked for it in the Antarctic Peninsula was 25 years ago.

"One could be misled to think that: Well, that was a unique thing that happened back in 2001, and nothing's happened ever since," says Vanstreels. Instead, it is possible that avian cholera die-offs could be occurring regularly, only scientists haven't been checking.

One of his big takeaways from this bird-flu-that-turned-out-to-be-avian-cholera event?

"Yes, there is a big thing with bird flu. But we still want to keep checking for the other diseases because they might be mixing up in the middle," Vanstreels says.

Antarctica isn't as remote as it seems

Like any good mystery, the case of the cholera-stricken penguins has got scientists wondering: Whodunit?

There's a theory that avian cholera might have been introduced to Antarctica decades ago from researchers who brought poultry from the U.S., Vanstreels says.

Gamble, of Cornell University, adds that the strain of avian cholera found in penguins in Antarctica is "very close" to the strain found 5,000 miles away on Île Amsterdam in the Southern Indian Ocean.

"Antarctica is way more connected to the rest of the world than we think it is," she says.

It's hard to track diseases in Antarctica but, she says, it's turning out to be an important piece in the global pathogen puzzle.

The work of keeping tabs on what's happening has fallen to a number of different countries since Antarctica is not governed by any one government. It was designated as a continent of peace and science by the mid 20th-century Antarctic Treaty, which now has 58 parties — among them are the U.S., France, Japan and Russia. Many nations have research stations and team up on scientific undertakings, including tracking pathogens — be it bird flu or avian cholera — that travel great distances and don't respect borders.

"So this Avian cholera outbreak is just showing this is not a unique event," says Gamble. "We really need international collaboration."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Lost your spark? The "silent sister" of depression, and a quiz to spot her
entries.summary: Always busy, but rarely joyful? Allison Aubrey and Juana Summers discuss a tool to spot "high functioning depression."
entries.content:
Some people with clinical depression can't get out of bed. But what about those who exhibit other signs of depression who never stop moving, and may double down on their work?

Psychiatrist Dr. Judith Joseph says the second group often goes unnoticed, even by the people living it. She calls it "high-functioning depression": people who keep meeting their obligations at work and at home while quietly losing the ability to feel pleasure.

"When you are joyful, you have better physical health, you have better relationships, you have better productivity at work," Joseph said in an interview for the Your Turn podcast. "So why don't we prioritize it?"

At the center of Joseph's work is anhedonia: a reduced ability to feel joy, pleasure or interest in things that once brought those feelings. Joseph describes it as "the silent sister" of depression.

"One sister is depressed, and crying, and not getting out of bed, and getting all the attention," she says. "The other one is quiet and numb." Anhedonia may not seem like a crisis in the classic sense, Joseph says. "But it is an existential crisis, and it's not something to ignore."

What the research shows

In a peer-reviewed study published in the journal Cureus, Joseph and colleagues interviewed adults using a set of questionnaires designed to assess high-functioning depression, trauma and anhedonia.

The results supported the researchers' hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Participants with higher anhedonia scores also had higher high-functioning depression scores.

Parents and caregivers had the highest anhedonia and high-functioning depression scores in the study.

The authors note that high-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5, the manual clinicians use to diagnose mental health conditions. They say that is part of the problem: people who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they reach burnout.

'Something's gonna give'

Joseph says she often sees the pattern in women who are the steady presence for everyone around them. They are so focused on their responsibilities at work and at home that they don't realize they are burned out, or close to it.

"But eventually something's gonna give," she said. "Either they do break down and they have a clinical depression and they lose their functioning, they go into distress or crisis, or they physically break down."

She said she has seen patients end up in the emergency room without understanding why, only to learn they had been carrying unresolved emotional pain.

Joseph said the pattern is common in professions that discourage vulnerability, including her own. In medicine, she said, crying after a patient died was seen as weakness.

"In medicine, we focus on the crisis," Joseph said. "You're [taught] to look for the mania, for the psychosis." She believes there should be more focus on anhedonia, the loss of sense of joy.

A self-assessment

Joseph developed an anhedonia quiz based on the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale, a measure of the capacity to feel pleasure that was published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

The questionnaire asks about everyday experiences, such as whether you have trouble enjoying praise, whether you savor your meals or other small pleasures, and whether you struggle to enjoy your work or accomplishments because they never feel good enough.

The quiz is not a diagnostic tool. It's an invitation to take stock of what might be standing in the way of a fuller, more joyful life. If you'd like to take the quiz, you'll be asked to share your email to see the results.

Five V's

In her book, "High Functioning: Overcome Your Hidden Depression and Reclaim Your Joy," Joseph also outlines a framework she calls the Five V's:

  • Validation: naming and accepting what you feel.
  • Venting: expressing emotions, through talking, writing, creative expression or maybe a good cry.
  • Values: making time for what matters most.
  • Vision: having something to look forward to.
  • Vitals: caring for your whole self (mind + body) through sleep, nutrition and movement.

Joseph says anhedonia appears across many conditions, in many people in midlife and other times, too. "It's something that we need to learn how to detect," she said, because it can be a silent problem.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988, to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Want to know more? Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

entries.title: Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
entries.summary: A species of seabirds appears to become disoriented on flights back to its nest due to shifting time zones.
entries.content:
Even birds get jet lagged, study shows

New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.

A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.

Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.

Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.

For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.

Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.

Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?

To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.

He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.

"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.

In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.

That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.

"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.

Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.

"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.

entries.title: Fishing is a key issue in Alaska's tight U.S. Senate race
entries.summary: Alaska's U.S. Senate race is embroiled in an emotional fight over fish. Many in the state rely upon salmon to feed their families but those fish and others are increasingly hard to find.
entries.content:
Fishing is a key issue in Alaska's tight US Senate race

Alaska's U.S. Senate race is embroiled in an emotional fight over fish. Many in the state rely upon salmon to feed their families but those fish and others are increasingly hard to find.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

President Trump is trying to preemptively block election results in Alaska if the Republican incumbent loses. But in that state, the big issue in the Senate race has been an emotional fight over fish. And that's because the salmon that have long sustained Indigenous people are not returning to some Western Alaska rivers. While people living in remote villages feel the loss of salmon most acutely, the issue could ultimately affect the balance of power thousands of miles away in Washington, D.C. Alaska public media's Liz Ruskin reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOG BARKING)

LIZ RUSKIN, BYLINE: Evon Waska lives at the water's edge, where he says his parents settled when they gave up their nomadic life.

EVON WASKA: Well, this is my smokehouse, and this is where we make smoke, right?

RUSKIN: Waska's drying racks should be filled with salmon, but they're empty. Most years now, too few salmon return from the Bering Sea to his river, the Kuskokwim. To conserve fish, government agencies often close the river to fishing, even to those like Waska who fish to feed their families. Waska blames trawlers, industrial fishing boats miles offshore.

WASKA: They don't close the trawlers. They close me and my people first.

RUSKIN: Waska is up against a $1 billion industry, much of it based in Seattle. Picture a sock-shaped net that's a quarter mile long with an opening as wide as a football field. That's what trawlers tow to catch pollock. The white fish is served to you as imitation crab in McDonald's Filet-O-Fish. But also scooped up in those nets are prized king salmon and other fish. They're caught by accident and wasted, a problem known as bycatch. Alaskans are increasingly angry about it. Now, in a year where Alaska could decide the balance of power in the U.S. Senate, fish are all over political ads here.

(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: Senator Sullivan is championing legislation to reduce bycatch and strengthen Alaska's fisheries. Call Senator Dan Sullivan. Thank him and tell him to keep fighting for Alaska fishermen.

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: Dan Sullivan is taking big money from out-of-state corporate trawlers.

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #3: Mary Peltola tells a lot of fish tales to get votes.

RUSKIN: Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been an ally of the pollock industry. But this year, he's touting a new bill.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DAN SULLIVAN: It's the most comprehensive bycatch legislation ever to reduce bycatch, protect seafloor habitat.

RUSKIN: Democratic Senate challenger Mary Peltola is Indigenous, from the Kuskokwim. She says she'd ban factory trawlers, the largest of the pollock fleet. She calls Sullivan's bill an election year ploy.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARY PELTOLA: Dan Sullivan reeled in over $300,000 from trawlers and waited until the 11th hour for a half-hearted and half-baked solution.

RUSKIN: Heather Mann (ph) leads a trawlers association. She says scapegoating the pollock fishery won't help western Alaska.

HEATHER MANN: Even if you were to eliminate pollock, the chances of salmon runs being restored, what the science shows us is it would have a minimal impact.

RUSKIN: So far this year, pollock trawlers say they've caught 40,000 Alaska salmon. The waste is a tiny percentage of the massive pollock harvest.

(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE WHIRRING)

RUSKIN: But in the Kuskokwim River village of Kwethluk, it's galling.

(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE RUMBLING)

RUSKIN: Subsistence fishing is the main occupation here and the backbone of the culture. Tribal president Mary Nikolai steps into a neighbor's cold smokehouse. It pains her to see it was unused all summer.

MARY NICOLAI: Most of the smokehouses are like this. And it's like a slow trend of closing our workforce out.

RUSKIN: Regardless of who wins, she hopes this close Senate race tells the world of the threat they face.

For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Kwethluk, Alaska.

entries.title: US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production
entries.summary: The announcement Wednesday is the latest action by the allies, who have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
entries.content:
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.

It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.

Koizumi renews concern over China's naval activity

Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.

Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.

The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.

Japan, US to bolster joint missile production capacity

The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.

During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."

"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.

Hegseth reassures US engagement in the region

Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.

"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."

His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.

Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.

Australia shows commitment to defend the rule of law in the Pacific

Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.

"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."

The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.

Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.

Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

entries.title: China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline
entries.summary: This move comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is expected to secure his fourth five-year term.
entries.content:
China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline

BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.

The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.

During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.

The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.

Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.

The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."

It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.

The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.

Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.

Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.

The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.
